extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, biologists, and educated readers interested in evolutionary theory and the logic of natural selection
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for judging whether complex organs, structures, or habits can be explained by natural selection and descent with modification. Emphasises what evidence, mechanisms, and cautions make an evolutionary explanation plausible or problematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of numerous graduated intermediate stages
rubrics_metrics.description: If numerous gradations from a perfect and complex eye to one very imperfect and simple, each grade being useful to its possessor, can be shown to exist, then formation by natural selection is plausible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin emphasises that to accept formation of a complex organ by selection one should be able to show a series of slight, useful intermediate stages. He illustrates with eyes across Articulata and notes absence of such grades in Vertebrata/fossils is not decisive. The practical guidance: seek morphological series (lineal or collateral) demonstrating useful intermediates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation must be slight and heritable
rubrics_metrics.description: The eye does vary ever so slightly, and the variations be inherited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection requires small inheritable variations. The text stresses both the presence of slight variation and its transmission to offspring; without both, cumulative selection cannot operate. Look for evidence of heritable variation in the trait under study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Each intermediate grade must be useful to its possessor
rubrics_metrics.description: Each grade being useful to its possessor (i.e. each step confers some advantage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural selection acts on usefulness: intermediate forms must confer selectable benefit in the organism's environment. When evaluating proposed transitions, test whether each step would plausibly increase survival/reproduction under realistic conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection acts by numerous successive slight modifications (no jumps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural selection can act only by taking advantage of slight successive variations; she can never take a leap ('Natura non facit saltum').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject hypotheses that require abrupt, large-scale leaps in structure. Explanations should be decomposed into many small, selectable changes. Absence of intermediate forms may be due to extinction or rarity, not necessary jumps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek gradations in lineal ancestors or collateral descendants
rubrics_metrics.description: In looking for the gradations by which an organ in any species has been perfected, we ought to look exclusively to its lineal ancestors; but this is scarcely ever possible, and we are forced ... to look to species of the same group, that is to the collateral descendants ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When direct ancestors are unavailable, use related species (collateral lines) to infer possible transitional states and inherited modifications. Comparative anatomy across close relatives is legitimate evidence for possible gradations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of transitional fossils is not decisive (extinction & rarity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The chance of discovering species with transitional grades of structure in a fossil condition will always be less, from their having existed in lesser numbers, than in the case of species with fully developed structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret gaps in the fossil record cautiously: transitional stages may have been rare, short-lived, or supplanted and thus unlikely to be preserved. Do not treat fossil absence as definitive disproof of gradual evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organs can be converted from one function to another
rubrics_metrics.description: An organ originally constructed for one purpose (e.g. flotation) may be converted into one for a wholly different purpose (e.g. respiration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate homologies and developmental possibilities that permit functional shifts (e.g. swimbladder ↔ lung; ovigerous frena ↔ branchiæ). Demonstrate plausible intermediate modifications and selective advantages during conversion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple organs performing same function facilitate specialization
rubrics_metrics.description: Two distinct organs sometimes perform simultaneously the same function in the same individual; in these cases, one organ might with ease be modified and perfected so as to perform all the work by itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing origin of a novel organ/function, look for cases where redundancy or dual-function structures could allow one part to specialize while the other aids the transition (e.g. branchiæ and swimbladder).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider non-selective causes of small or seemingly useless characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters may have originated from climate, food, law of reversion, correlation of growth, or sexual selection—independently of direct natural selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not automatically attribute every trivial or puzzling trait to adaptive selection. Consider developmental constraints, pleiotropy, sexual selection, correlated variation, reversion, and direct physical effects as alternative or contributing causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some current trivial structures were once important in ancestors
rubrics_metrics.description: Organs now of trifling importance have probably in some cases been of high importance to an early progenitor, and after having been slowly perfected at a former period, have been transmitted in nearly the same state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a structure appears functionless, evaluate its evolutionary history—it may be a retained ancestral adaptation. Example: tail or limb bones inherited from aquatic ancestors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homology indicates inheritance from a common ancestor
rubrics_metrics.description: All physiologists admit that the swimbladder is homologous, or 'ideally similar,' in position and structure with the lungs of the higher vertebrate animals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use homology (similarity of position, structure, development) as evidence for common descent and for tracing functional shifts. Homologous structures across taxa support inheritance-based explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergence and parallelism are possible explanations for similar anomalous organs
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural selection, working for the good of each being and taking advantage of analogous variations, has sometimes modified in very nearly the same manner two parts in two organic beings, which owe but little of their structure in common to inheritance from the same ancestor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When similar unusual organs occur in distantly related taxa, consider independent evolution via analogous selection pressures rather than only shared ancestry. Look for subtle fundamental differences despite superficial similarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rare or scattered occurrence of an organ raises special difficulties but is not disproof
rubrics_metrics.description: The electric organs occur in only about a dozen fishes, of which several are widely remote in their affinities; this offers a difficulty but not an impossibility for selection-based explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat sparse phylogenetic distributions (e.g. electric organs, luminous organs) as challenging cases requiring special hypotheses (independent origin, deep ancestral loss), not automatic refutation of gradual evolution. Examine detailed structure for clues to origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection acts on the balance of good vs evil for the individual
rubrics_metrics.description: If a fair balance be struck between the good and evil caused by each part, each will be found on the whole advantageous. Natural selection will never produce in a being anything injurious to itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate traits by net fitness effect. Costs (e.g. bee sting that causes self-death) can be tolerated if overall advantage to the individual or colony outweighs costs. Consider community-level or inclusive-fitness explanations where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural selection tends to relative, not absolute, perfection
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural selection tends only to make each organic being as perfect as, or slightly more perfect than, the other inhabitants of the same country with which it has to struggle for existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect optimal or absolute designs; expect adaptations relative to contemporaneous competitors and environments. Use empirical measures of comparative performance rather than idealized perfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware inferring current adaptive purpose from present structure alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Habits have changed without a corresponding change of structure ... The webbed feet of the upland goose may be said to have become rudimentary in function, though not in structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between present function, ancestral function, and structural retention. Functional inference should consider ecology, behaviour, and ancestral states; avoid assuming current utility from morphology alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrability condition — failure of the criterion would falsify the theory
rubrics_metrics.description: If it could be demonstrated that any complex organ existed, which could not possibly have been formed by numerous, successive, slight modifications, my theory would absolutely break down.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat as a strong falsifiability criterion: identify organs or structures for which no plausible series of slight, useful steps (given variation and inheritance) can be outlined. These would pose genuine challenges to the selection hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanistic plausibility via comparison, development, and microstructure
rubrics_metrics.description: No one will dispute that the ovigerous frena in the one family are strictly homologous with the branchiæ of the other family; indeed, they graduate into each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use detailed morphological, developmental, and microanatomical comparisons to show gradations and plausible mechanistic pathways (e.g., glands/skin folds → respiratory filaments). Concrete structural continuity strengthens evolutionary explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplication of variants by many individuals and generations enables selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Variation will cause the slight alterations, generation will multiply them almost infinitely, and natural selection will pick out with unerring skill each improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether population size, generation time, and heritability suffice to produce and amplify the necessary variants. The telescope analogy: many trials (individuals) over many generations allow selection to accumulate small improvements.
